AHBM: Just ten companies: Asia's biggest memory chip makers, the firms in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan whose chips store data for AI servers and phones. Memory is a boom-and-bust business, and with only ten names this is among the most concentrated ways to bet on it.
ALRG: Large US companies picked with a disciplined mix of fundamental research and valuation work, hunting for high-quality firms priced below what their growth is worth. It is a core-style holding led by technology at over two-fifths, aiming to beat the broad market modestly over time.
ARLI: Options on developed-market stocks outside the US that absorb the first 15% of losses over a period ending each April, the level in its name, with no cap on gains above a threshold. Skipping the cap leaves more upside than most buffer funds, paid for in the structure's other terms.
ARMY: Aerospace and defense companies from around the world: jet and missile makers, shipbuilders and military electronics firms, across allied nations. It is a focused bet on the global rearmament cycle, with especially strong tailwinds in Europe, plus the currency and political risks of foreign markets.
BILD: Listed infrastructure companies worldwide: electric and gas utilities at about half, plus toll roads, airports, pipelines and water systems. These assets collect regulated or contracted fees from essential services, so the fund aims for steady income and moderate growth with defensive traits.
BRKC: Options built around a single stock, Berkshire Hathaway's Class B shares, paired with Treasury bills held as collateral. It sells call options to turn a famously steady conglomerate's moves into regular payouts, capping the gains when the stock climbs, so it is an income play, not ownership.
BSTS: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2028, held in a fund designed to wind up at the end of that year and return the cash. It works like owning a single bond with a known end date, paying government-backed income with rate risk that fades as 2028 nears.
BUFE: Four emerging-market buffer funds staggered through the year, each absorbing the first slice of losses on developing-market stocks over its own period while capping gains. It softens a famously volatile corner of the market, with protection renewing quarterly instead of once a year.
DDDD: Dividend-leaning US stocks across staples, health care, technology and energy, paired with options sold to roughly double the distribution rate a plain stock fund would pay, as its name promises. Bigger payouts mean more upside handed to option buyers when stocks rally.
DGAP: Options on the S&P 500 that pay a preset digital return if the market is flat, up, or down only a little over the year ending in April, with a buffer for small losses. Bigger drops pass through beyond the buffer, so it suits investors happy with a fixed modest gain.
DRMY: Memory chip companies, the makers of the DRAM and flash storage inside every computer and AI server, paired with options that convert their swings into income. Memory prices cycle violently between shortage and glut, so the income comes attached to a very bumpy ride.
EMDV: Emerging-market companies that have raised their dividends for at least seven straight years, led by banks and technology firms across Asia and beyond. It pairs developing-world growth with an income discipline, favoring proven payers in markets where dividends are less common.
EPIN: Companies across developed markets outside the US, in Europe, Japan and elsewhere, picked actively across technology, industry and banking. It is a core foreign stock holding with a manager's hand on stock selection, adding diversification and currency swings to a US-heavy portfolio.
ESMV: Large and mid-sized US companies chosen for two traits: steadier prices than the market and better environmental and social scores with lower carbon output. It is a defensive core holding with a values screen, designed to fall less in sell-offs while avoiding the worst polluters.
ETFT: A concentrated portfolio of high-quality global companies, household names in technology, health care and consumer goods, bought to hold for years. The manager famously does almost nothing once invested, so it is a patient compounder fund whose results rest on picking great businesses and never selling.
EVMT: Futures on the metals electric vehicles are made from: copper, aluminum, nickel, cobalt, lithium and iron ore, held through a structure that avoids the K-1 tax form. It bets on raw material prices rather than miners, so it adds futures roll costs and commodity swings without company risk.
FSEV: Small, cheap US companies from the Russell 2000 Value index, tilted by Fidelity's research toward the ones it rates most attractive. It plays the small-value role, a corner that has beaten the market over long stretches but can lag for years when growth stocks are fashionable.
GAVA: Direct ownership of AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain, with the holdings staked to help run the network and earn extra tokens. It wraps a single mid-sized cryptocurrency in a fund, so expect swings larger than bitcoin's, with staking rewards adding a little on top.
HAUS: Real estate investment trusts that own homes and apartments: big apartment landlords and single-family rental companies. It is a bet on housing and rents rather than offices or malls, paying property income while rising and falling with rent growth and interest rates.
IOPP: Indian companies picked actively by a specialist manager, leaning toward consumer brands at about two-fifths as India's middle class spends more. It is a single-country growth bet with local expertise, carrying India's currency swings and its market's rich valuations.
JUDO: US stocks across technology, banking, health care and media, paired with options sold to enhance the income the portfolio pays. It aims to behave like a core stock holding with fatter payouts, giving up a slice of strong rallies to fund them.
KDVD: Dividend-paying companies of all sizes, spread across banking, consumer brands, industry and technology, picked by a long-running value shop. It aims for income plus steady growth from proven payers, playing a middle role between pure yield funds and growth funds.
MFUL: A conservative all-in-one mix, roughly four-tenths stocks and the rest mostly bonds, spread across sizes, countries and credit qualities. It aims for gentle growth with smaller drops than a stock fund, suiting cautious investors who still need some return above inflation.
MUNA: Municipal bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at the year 2030, paying tax-free interest and gradually returning principal through regular distributions. It suits a goal at the end of this decade, with federal tax-free income along the way and risk that shrinks as the ladder shortens.
MUNC: Municipal bonds arranged in a ladder aimed at the year 2045, paying tax-free interest and gradually returning principal through regular distributions. It is built for savers who want a bond portfolio that pays itself out over time toward a distant goal, with federal tax-free income along the way.
MYCP: Corporate bonds from US companies that mostly come due in 2036, held as a date-targeted income portfolio. It suits money aimed at a goal around 2036: interest payments along the way, company credit risk throughout, and rate risk that fades as the due dates approach.
MYMH: Municipal bonds from US states and cities that mostly come due in 2028, paying interest that is exempt from regular federal income tax. It suits savers aiming at a goal around 2028, with tax-free income along the way and risk that eases as the bonds near their due dates.
NFLW: Magnified exposure to a single stock, streaming giant Netflix, built from swaps and shares to deliver about 1.2 times its weekly move, plus weekly distributions. The weekly reset makes longer results drift from that multiple, so it is a short-term trading tool on one very popular stock.
NUKX: Nuclear energy companies, uranium miners, reactor builders and the utilities that run power plants, paired with options that turn their moves into income. It is a bet on nuclear's comeback for clean, always-on power, with payouts added by the options program.
PMJL: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb as much loss as the structure allows over a one-year period ending in July, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the most defensive version of a buffer fund, suiting investors who fear a down year more than they want full upside.
PMSE: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb as much loss as the structure allows over a one-year period ending in September, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is the most defensive version of a buffer fund, suiting investors who fear a down year more than they want full upside.
QBIF: Options on developed-market stocks outside the US, mostly Europe and Japan, that absorb the first 15% of losses over each outcome period, the level in its name, while capping gains. It is a cushioned core foreign holding for investors who want overseas diversification with softer drops.
QBIV: Options on developed-market stocks outside the US, mostly Europe and Japan, that absorb the first 5% of losses over each outcome period, the level in its name, while capping gains. It is a defensive way to hold foreign stocks, trading some upside for a modest cushion against down periods abroad.
QBKF: Options on US small-company stocks that absorb the first 15% of losses over each outcome period, the level in its name, while capping gains. Small caps swing harder than big ones, so the cushion is the appeal, bought by giving up the strongest rallies.
QBKV: Options on US small-company stocks that absorb the first 5% of losses over each outcome period, the level in its name, while capping gains. The cushion here is thinner than in 15% buffer funds, which leaves more upside but less protection when small caps slide.
RHTX: A tactical mix of other funds that can swing from all stocks to all bonds as the adviser's market outlook changes. It is a hands-off allocation fund whose results depend on the manager's timing calls, which can protect in slumps or lag badly in sudden rallies.
RYLG: Small US companies of the Russell 2000 paired with call options sold against the portfolio for income. Unlike full covered call funds, part of the portfolio is left uncovered to keep more growth, so payouts are smaller but the small-cap upside is less capped.
SAWS: Small US companies picked for quality and growth: profitable firms with strong balance sheets that are still expanding, led by health care and industry. It is an active small-cap growth holding that tries to avoid the flimsiest small stocks, though the size range still swings hard.
SIMS: Companies building intelligent infrastructure: smart grids, connected buildings, efficient water and transport systems, mostly industrial and technology firms. It is a bet on the world's roads, wires and pipes getting sensors and software, a steadier cousin of pure tech funds.
SJCP: Core bonds with extras: investment-grade corporate and government debt and mortgage bonds, plus a large slice of preferred stocks for added yield. It plays the core bond role with more income reach, accepting extra credit and rate risk from the preferred and mortgage corners.
SPAM: Cybersecurity companies worldwide: the software and services firms that defend networks, cloud systems and data from attack. Spending on digital defense keeps growing whatever the economy does, but these are still richly priced tech stocks that swing with the sector's mood.
SPXD: The same 500 companies as the famous index, but reweighted so no single industry or giant stock dominates: technology shrinks to about a sixth. It keeps big-company diversification while muting the mega-cap concentration that now drives the standard index, a quieter version of a core holding.
TSES: US companies tied to American energy security: oil and gas producers, utilities and the industrial firms that build energy infrastructure. It is a patriotic-flavored energy bet that leans on domestic production and grid strength, swinging with energy prices and policy.
TXCA: California municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, paying interest exempt from both federal and California state income tax for residents. It is a tax-focused income holding for Californians, with all its eggs in one state's finances and water, transport and school projects.
TXNY: New York municipal bonds with intermediate maturities, paying interest exempt from federal, state and, for city residents, New York City income tax. It is a tax-focused income holding for New Yorkers, concentrated in one state's schools, transit, water and housing projects.
USE: Bets on energy prices themselves, oil, gasoline and natural gas futures and options, shifted around by a proprietary model that can bet for or against prices. It aims for returns that do not depend on the stock market, with commodity swings and model risk instead.
VEM: Dividend-paying companies across emerging markets, led by Asian technology giants and banks, chosen for income as well as growth. It is a steadier take on developing markets, favoring established payers, though currency swings and political risk still come with the territory.
WEED: Companies across the cannabis and hemp business: growers, medical marijuana firms, retailers and the landlords that rent to them. Legalization politics drive this young industry, so the fund is a speculative bet on the patchwork of state and national rules loosening further.
WSDB: Short-term bonds from governments and companies, mostly high quality, with room for a small slice of lower-rated debt for extra yield. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it plays the defensive income role for money that cannot afford much drama.
XLBI: Chemical makers, miners, packaging and metals companies from the S&P 500, paired with an options program that adds premium income. Materials pay decent dividends and swing with commodity prices, so this stacks option payouts on a cyclical sector bet.
